newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: Goldman Sachs says NZ easing not enough - NZPA.
newsitem.headline: Goldman Sachs says NZ easing not enough - NZPA.

text.p: A fall in interest rates and currency after comments by Governor Don Brash on Thursday does not ease monetary conditions enough, according to United States investment bank Goldman Sachs.
Chief currency dealer Jim O'Neill told the New Zealand Press Association on Friday the market-led easing was "not sufficient".
"I can understand why the Reserve Bank is being cautious, but it's kind of nonsensical really," O'Neill said.

According to Goldman's calculations the Reserve Bank's own inflation forecasts suggested short term interest rates could be down below five percent -- below United States rates -- by the end of the year.

After comments by Reserve Bank governor Don Brash which were seen by the markets to have an easing bias, the currency dipped about 30 basis points to close at US$0.6903 on Thursday. The kiwi was at 0.6897 in early trade on Friday.

Rates on 90-day bank bills closed at 6.94 percent from 7.03 percent immediately before Brash's comments, and were at 6.92 percent early today. On a trade-weighted basis, the kiwi on Friday was at 68.39, having slipped to 68.6 from 68.9 on Thursday.
Brash had said monetary conditions were slightly firmer than assumed in the bank's March economic forecast, despite recent weak economic data.
O'Neill told NZPA it was inevitable the bank would move slowly towards having short-term interest rates below five percent.
"It's highly likely that, as I believe they hinted overnight, that at the next (June) statement they will shift to an easier monetary conditions stance."
O'Neill said he would not be surprised if Thursday's movements were at least endorsed. An endorsement could be for interest rates at current levels, but the TWI "somewhat lower".

"Don Brash has made it pretty clear that he would be perfectly happy for interest rates to rise elsewhere and New Zealand rates to not (rise), in order that the interest rate differential narrows, and the kiwi does drop. I think he's going to get what he wants."
While the bank would be looking to achieve a lower dollar, with the recent pessimism shown in business surveys it would also be happy to see interest rates fall, he said.
New Zealand had suffered from the strong exchange rate, which was overvalued as much as 15 percent.
O'Neill strongly disagreed with those who supported caution based on the supposed inflationary impact of upcoming increased government spending.
